title: Bonding, Structure and Properties of Materials
seo_title: Year 11 Chemistry: Bonding and Properties of Materials Worksheets (Australian Curriculum)
standard_code: Chemistry Unit 1: Properties and structure of materials
standard_text: Ionic, covalent (molecular and network) and metallic bonding and the properties they explain; alloys and nanomaterials; shapes of molecules (VSEPR); writing formulae; separating mixtures by filtration, distillation and chromatography. (Senior Secondary Chemistry, Unit 1: Chemical fundamentals: structure, properties and reactions)
meta_desc: Free Year 11 Chemistry worksheets on bonding and materials: ionic, covalent and metallic bonds, lattices, diamond and graphite, alloys, nanomaterials, VSEPR shapes, formulae and separation. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Ionic: ion lattice. Metallic: cations in a sea of electrons. Covalent: shared pairs.
body_html:
How to think about it

Ionic compounds are lattices of ions: high melting points, brittle, conduct only when molten or dissolved. Metals are cations in a sea of delocalised electrons: conductive and malleable. Covalent substances are either small molecules (low melting points) or giant networks such as diamond and silicon dioxide (very high melting points).

VSEPR theory: electron pairs around the central atom repel, giving shapes such as linear, bent, trigonal pyramidal and tetrahedral. Mixtures are separated using differences in particle size, boiling point or attraction to a stationary phase.

Example

Shape of NH₃?

3 bonding pairs + 1 lone pair

tetrahedral arrangement, one corner empty

Answer: trigonal pyramidal

Example

Formula of aluminium oxide?

Al³⁺ and O²⁻

2 × (+3) = 3 × (−2)

Answer: Al₂O₃

Common mistakes

  • Saying ionic solids conduct electricity: the ions cannot move.
  • Breaking covalent bonds when a molecular substance melts: only the intermolecular forces are overcome.
  • Ignoring lone pairs when working out a shape.

faq.q: Why does sodium chloride conduct when dissolved but not when solid?
faq.a: In the solid the ions are fixed in the lattice; in solution (or molten) they are free to move and carry charge.
Their tiny particles have a huge surface area to volume ratio, so they can be more reactive, stronger or transparent, as in sunscreens and catalysts.

items.q: What kind of bond forms between iron (Fe) and sodium (Na)?
items.e: Metal atoms share a sea of electrons.

items.q: Why do ionic compounds conduct electricity when molten but not when solid?
c: the ions are free to move only when molten or dissolved
solid ionic compounds have no ions
items.e: In the solid the ions are fixed in the lattice.

items.q: Why does diamond have a very high melting point?
c: each carbon is covalently bonded to four others in a giant network
it has weak forces between molecules
items.e: All the strong covalent bonds must be broken.

items.q: What kind of bond forms between nitrogen (N) and sulfur (S)?
items.e: Two non-metals share electrons.

items.q: What kind of bond forms between iron (Fe) and iodine (I)?
items.e: A metal gives electrons to a non-metal.

items.q: What kind of bond forms between sodium (Na) and tin (Sn)?
items.e: Metal atoms share a sea of electrons.

items.q: Why are metals malleable?
c: layers of cations can slide over each other while the delocalised electrons keep holding them together
the ions repel each other strongly
items.e: Metallic bonding is not directional.

items.q: Ba<sup>2+</sup> and F<sup>−</sup> ions combine. What is the formula of the compound?
items.e: Use the lowest numbers that make the total charge zero: 1 × (+2) + 2 × (−1) = 0.

items.q: Na<sup>+</sup> and N<sup>3−</sup> ions combine. What is the formula of the compound?
items.e: Use the lowest numbers that make the total charge zero: 3 × (+1) + 1 × (−3) = 0.

items.q: What is an alloy?
c: a mixture of a metal with other elements, such as steel (iron and carbon)
items.e: Different-sized atoms stop layers sliding, so alloys are harder.

items.q: What kind of bond forms between zinc (Zn) and nitrogen (N)?
items.e: A metal gives electrons to a non-metal.

items.q: What kind of bond forms between bromine (Br) and fluorine (F)?
items.e: Two non-metals share electrons.

items.q: Why is an alloy usually harder than the pure metal?
c: atoms of different sizes disrupt the layers so they cannot slide easily
items.e: Bronze and steel are harder than copper and iron.

items.q: What kind of bond forms between copper (Cu) and silver (Ag)?
items.e: Metal atoms share a sea of electrons.

items.q: What is the formula of strontium chloride?
items.e: Strontium forms Sr<sup>2+</sup> and chlorine forms Cl<sup>−</sup>; the charges must add to zero.

items.q: Li<sup>+</sup> and S<sup>2−</sup> ions combine. What is the formula of the compound?
items.e: Use the lowest numbers that make the total charge zero: 2 × (+1) + 1 × (−2) = 0.

items.q: What is the formula of strontium iodide?
items.e: Strontium forms Sr<sup>2+</sup> and iodine forms I<sup>−</sup>; the charges must add to zero.

items.q: What is the formula of strontium fluoride?
items.e: Strontium forms Sr<sup>2+</sup> and fluorine forms F<sup>−</sup>; the charges must add to zero.

items.q: Why do metals conduct electricity?
c: they have a sea of delocalised electrons that can move through the lattice
their ions move to the electrodes
items.e: Electrons carry the charge.

items.q: What kind of bond forms between magnesium (Mg) and aluminium (Al)?
items.e: Metal atoms share a sea of electrons.

items.q: Which substance conducts electricity when molten but not when solid?
items.e: Ions are fixed in the solid but free to move when molten.

items.q: What is graphene?
c: a single layer of carbon atoms in a hexagonal network
items.e: It is very strong and conducts electricity.

items.q: A polymer chain is made of 5000 units of propene (C₃H₆, 42 g/mol). About what is its molar mass?
Which monomer is linked to make starch or cellulose?
items.e: Polymers are chains of repeating monomers.

items.q: Which monomer is linked to make PVC (pipes)?
items.e: Polymers are chains of repeating monomers.

items.q: What kind of structure does iodine have?
items.e: Weak van der Waals forces between I₂ molecules, so it sublimes easily.

items.q: How can pure water be obtained from sea water?
items.e: Water evaporates and condenses; salt is left behind.

items.q: Many ethene monomers are linked in a long chain. Which polymer forms?
items.e: Polymers are chains of repeating monomers.

items.q: Why does diamond have a very high melting point?
c: many strong covalent bonds must be broken
items.e: Diamond is a giant covalent (macromolecular) structure.

items.q: Why do ionic compounds have high melting points?
c: strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions in a lattice must be overcome
the covalent bonds inside molecules are strong
items.e: Every ion is attracted to many neighbours.

items.q: How can ethanol be separated from water?
c: fractional distillation, because their boiling points are different
items.e: Ethanol boils at 78 °C, water at 100 °C.

items.q: Why does graphite conduct electricity but diamond does not?
c: each carbon in graphite bonds to three others, leaving one delocalised electron
items.e: The electrons move along the layers.

items.q: Which monomer is linked to make proteins?
items.e: Polymers are chains of repeating monomers.

items.q: Which type of bonding is found in water molecules?
items.e: Non-metals share electron pairs.

items.q: Which molecule has polar bonds but is non-polar overall?
items.e: CO₂ is linear, so the two C=O dipoles cancel.

items.q: Why does water have a higher boiling point than H₂S?
items.e: Hydrogen bonds are stronger than the other intermolecular forces in H₂S.

items.q: A polymer chain is made of 1000 units of vinyl chloride (C₂H₃Cl, 62.5 g/mol). About what is its molar mass?
Why do the boiling points of the noble gases increase down the group?
c: there are more electrons, so van der Waals forces are stronger
items.e: Bigger atoms have bigger induced dipole–dipole forces.

items.q: Why do nanoparticles often behave differently from the bulk material?
c: they have a much larger surface area to volume ratio
they are made of different elements
items.e: Zinc oxide nanoparticles in sunscreen look clear, not white.

items.q: What is the strongest type of intermolecular force?
items.e: Covalent bonds are within molecules, not between them.

items.q: What is the shape of ClF<sub>3</sub>?
items.e: 3 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs around the central atom: T-shaped.

items.q: How can sand be separated from salt water?
items.e: Insoluble solids stay on the filter paper.

items.q: What is the shape of SiCl<sub>4</sub>?
items.e: 4 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs around the central atom: tetrahedral.

items.q: What is the bond angle in CO<sub>2</sub>?
items.e: 2 bonding pairs, 0 lone pairs. Lone pairs repel more than bonding pairs, so each lone pair closes the angle by about 2.5°.

items.q: What is the shape of BH<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup>?
items.e: 4 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs around the central atom: tetrahedral.

items.q: What is the shape of SF<sub>4</sub>?
items.e: 4 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair around the central atom: seesaw.

items.q: What is the bond angle in SiCl<sub>4</sub>?
items.e: 4 bonding pairs, 0 lone pairs. Lone pairs repel more than bonding pairs, so each lone pair closes the angle by about 2.5°.

items.q: What is the shape of CCl<sub>4</sub>?
items.e: 4 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs around the central atom: tetrahedral.

items.q: What is the shape of SF<sub>6</sub>?
items.e: 6 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs around the central atom: octahedral.

items.q: What is the shape of NH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup>?
items.e: 2 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs around the central atom: bent (non-linear).

items.q: What is the bond angle in NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>?
items.e: 4 bonding pairs, 0 lone pairs. Lone pairs repel more than bonding pairs, so each lone pair closes the angle by about 2.5°.

items.q: What is the shape of NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>?
items.e: 4 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs around the central atom: tetrahedral.

items.q: Crude oil is separated into fractions at a refinery. Which property is used?
items.e: Smaller hydrocarbons boil at lower temperatures.

items.q: What is a nanomaterial?
c: a material more than 1 mm thick
a material with particles or structures 1–100 nm in size
items.e: Nanoparticles have a very large surface area to volume ratio.

items.q: What is the shape of H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>?
items.e: 3 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair around the central atom: pyramidal.

items.q: How many lone pairs of electrons are on the central atom in SF<sub>4</sub>?
items.e: SF4: 4 bonding pairs and 1 lone pairs.

items.q: What is the shape of PH<sub>3</sub>?
items.e: 3 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair around the central atom: pyramidal.

items.q: What is the bond angle in H<sub>2</sub>O?
items.e: 2 bonding pairs, 2 lone pairs. Lone pairs repel more than bonding pairs, so each lone pair closes the angle by about 2.5°.

items.q: What does a high Rf value mean in paper chromatography?
c: the substance is more attracted to the paper
the substance is more attracted to the mobile phase and moves further
the substance is insoluble in the solvent
items.e: Rf = distance moved by spot ÷ distance moved by solvent.

items.q: What is the shape of BeCl<sub>2</sub>?
items.e: 2 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs around the central atom: linear.

items.q: Which type of bonding is found in sodium chloride?
items.e: A metal and a non-metal: electron transfer.

items.q: What is the name of Li<sub>2</sub>S?
items.e: Name the metal, then the non-metal with -ide. Ionic names do not use prefixes.

it is a good conductor and is ductile

items.q: Electronegativity: nitrogen (N) = 3.04 and germanium (Ge) = 2.01. What type of bond forms between them?
items.e: Difference = 1.03. Below 0.4: nonpolar; 0.4–1.7: polar covalent; above 1.7: ionic.
